variants.title: Serve one request
variants.context: A real-time inference path turns a live request into a decision inside one deadline: retrieve fresh features, select a model, run inference, apply business rules, record telemetry, and return or emit the result. Every stage spends the same budget.
variants.prompt: A ranking request arrives with a strict deadline. Put the stages of the serving path in order.

items.text: Apply business rules and thresholds to turn the score into a decision.
Select the model version that this request and its policy are eligible for.
Return the decision, or emit it downstream, within the caller's budget.
Run inference under a bounded call with a deadline of its own.
Retrieve fresh features for the entities in the request, using non-blocking calls.
Record latency, error, freshness, and saturation telemetry for the request.

variants.hint: Every stage in the path is spending the same deadline.
variants.explanation: The deadline covers feature retrieval, queueing, inference, policy, and serialization together, which is why optimizing the model call alone rarely fixes a tail.

variants.title: Serve one request
variants.context: A real-time inference path turns a live request into a decision inside one deadline: retrieve fresh features, select a model, run inference, apply business rules, record telemetry, and return or emit the result. Every stage spends the same budget.
variants.prompt: A fraud decision must be auditable and safe to retry. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Apply calibrated thresholds and rules, sending edge cases to human review.
Route to the calibrated model version recorded for this decision type.
Look up the entity's durable features together with the live transaction context.
Score the transaction inside its bounded time budget.
Return the decision so a retry reproduces it rather than creating a second action.
Write the decision with its reason path and an idempotency key.

variants.hint: An adverse action has to be explainable and repeatable later.
variants.explanation: Idempotency and an auditable reason path are part of the decision, so they are produced on the request path rather than reconstructed afterwards.

variants.title: Serve one request
variants.context: A real-time inference path turns a live request into a decision inside one deadline: retrieve fresh features, select a model, run inference, apply business rules, record telemetry, and return or emit the result. Every stage spends the same budget.
variants.prompt: An ETA service depends on a live feed that just started missing its deadline. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Return the bounded estimate inside the original deadline.
Apply the fallback estimate policy for a prediction made without fresh context.
Emit telemetry marking the degraded path and its feature freshness.
Request the fresh context feature with a timeout smaller than the product deadline.
Detect the miss and open the circuit breaker instead of waiting on the slow dependency.
Score with the durable entity features that are already available.

variants.hint: A fallback only helps if it is triggered before the deadline is already gone.
variants.explanation: Circuit breakers and fallbacks convert a slow dependency into a bounded, observable degradation instead of a timed-out request.

variants.title: Budget the stages
variants.context: Multi-stage systems give each stage its own budget. Retrieval narrows candidates before expensive ranking, policy runs last, and under deadline pressure the system degrades by skipping stages rather than timing out the request.
variants.prompt: A search ranker runs four stages under separate budgets. Put them in order.

items.text: Policy applies rules, filters, and presentation constraints to the ranked list.
Lexical retrieval produces an initial candidate set from the query.
Learned retrieval widens or refines those candidates with an embedding lookup.
The ranking model scores the reduced candidate set.

variants.hint: Expensive scoring only runs on what earlier stages let through.
variants.explanation: Each stage has its own budget so the costly ranker sees a small candidate set, which is what makes the total deadline achievable.

variants.title: Budget the stages
variants.context: Multi-stage systems give each stage its own budget. Retrieval narrows candidates before expensive ranking, policy runs last, and under deadline pressure the system degrades by skipping stages rather than timing out the request.
variants.prompt: A recommendation service must avoid an uncorrected feedback loop. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Rank the candidates with the heavier model inside its own budget.
Log which items were actually exposed to the user.
Generate a small candidate set before any expensive scoring runs.
Apply policy and diversity rules to the ranked list.
Join later clicks against that exposure log rather than against the full catalog.

variants.hint: Clicks only mean something relative to what the user could have seen.
variants.explanation: Logging exposure is what stops clicks from becoming an uncorrected feedback loop, because unseen items are not evidence of rejection.

variants.title: Budget the stages
variants.context: Multi-stage systems give each stage its own budget. Retrieval narrows candidates before expensive ranking, policy runs last, and under deadline pressure the system degrades by skipping stages rather than timing out the request.
variants.prompt: Load spikes and the ranker will not finish in budget. Put the degradation steps in order.

items.text: Skip learned retrieval and keep the cheaper candidate set already produced.
Emit telemetry naming which stages were skipped for this request.
Detect that the remaining budget cannot cover the next stage.
Score fewer candidates, or fall back to the lighter ranking path.
Still apply the policy stage so filters and constraints are not bypassed.

variants.hint: Degrading means returning less work, not returning it late.
variants.explanation: A multi-stage ranker degrades by skipping stages rather than timing out, and policy is the stage that must never be skipped silently.

variants.title: Do the latency math
variants.context: The performance model is explicit. Uncached latency is base latency times the hardware multiplier times the compression multiplier, cached latency is uncached latency times the cache latency factor, and effective throughput is the smaller of the requested rate and 1,000 divided by cached latency times the batch size.
variants.prompt: A model has a base latency of 40 ms. It runs on GPU with a hardware multiplier of 0.3, and high compression applies a multiplier of 0.6. What is the uncached latency?
variants.hint: Both multipliers apply to the same base figure.
variants.explanation: Uncached latency is base latency times the hardware multiplier times the compression multiplier, so the two effects compound rather than being chosen between.

mistakes.feedback: That applies the hardware multiplier alone and ignores compression.
That applies the compression multiplier alone and ignores the hardware.

variants.title: Do the latency math
variants.context: The performance model is explicit. Uncached latency is base latency times the hardware multiplier times the compression multiplier, cached latency is uncached latency times the cache latency factor, and effective throughput is the smaller of the requested rate and 1,000 divided by cached latency times the batch size.
variants.prompt: Uncached latency is 12 ms and the cache latency factor is 0.25. What is the cached latency?
variants.hint: The factor scales the latency down; it is not a saving to subtract.
variants.explanation: Cached latency is uncached latency times the cache latency factor, which is what makes hit rate the lever on how much traffic reaches the model fleet.

mistakes.feedback: That divides by the factor instead of multiplying by it.
That is the time saved by the cache, not the cached latency itself.

variants.title: Do the latency math
variants.context: The performance model is explicit. Uncached latency is base latency times the hardware multiplier times the compression multiplier, cached latency is uncached latency times the cache latency factor, and effective throughput is the smaller of the requested rate and 1,000 divided by cached latency times the batch size.
variants.prompt: Cached latency is 4 ms with a batch size of 32, and the caller requests 20,000 requests per second. What is the effective throughput?
variants.hint: Effective throughput cannot exceed what the path can actually serve.
variants.explanation: Effective throughput is the smaller of the requested rate and 1,000 divided by cached latency times the batch size, here 250 batches per second of 32 requests.

mistakes.feedback: That reports the requested rate without checking what the path can serve.
That is batches per second; each batch carries 32 requests.

variants.title: Choose the architecture
variants.context: Four architectures answer different questions. Request-response returns one decision before the caller's deadline. An event stream consumes durable events and emits predictions continuously. Micro-batching accumulates compatible requests under a bounded wait. Precompute or edge serves a recent prediction near the caller.
variants.prompt: Predictions are produced from a durable event log where ordering, replay, and idempotent output matter more than answering a caller. Which architecture fits?
options: Request-response, because each event still needs its own decision.
An event stream, consuming durable events and emitting predictions continuously.
Micro-batching, because events naturally arrive in groups.
optionFeedback: No caller is waiting, so a synchronous response contract adds constraints without value.
Correct: durable consumption replaces the synchronous deadline with ordering, replay, and idempotency concerns.
Bounded batching is a throughput tactic, not the consumption model this workload needs.
variants.hint: Ask whether anyone is holding a connection open waiting for this answer.
variants.explanation: An event-stream path trades the synchronous deadline for ordering, replay, state, and idempotent outputs, which are different correctness concerns.

variants.title: Choose the architecture
variants.context: Four architectures answer different questions. Request-response returns one decision before the caller's deadline. An event stream consumes durable events and emits predictions continuously. Micro-batching accumulates compatible requests under a bounded wait. Precompute or edge serves a recent prediction near the caller.
variants.prompt: Results are broadly reusable, key cardinality is low, and a prediction a few minutes old is still acceptable to the product. Which architecture fits?
options: Request-response, running the model fresh for every caller.
An event stream, so each update emits a new prediction downstream.
Precompute or edge, serving a recent prediction near the caller.
optionFeedback: Recomputing an identical answer per caller spends the deadline on work that is already known.
Emitting on every update does not by itself put the result close to the caller.
Correct: reusable low-cardinality results with tolerant freshness can be moved earlier and served near the caller.
variants.hint: Reusability and freshness tolerance are what make work movable earlier.
variants.explanation: Precompute and edge serving work when freshness and key cardinality permit, and then invalidation and versioned cache keys become correctness concerns.

variants.title: Choose the architecture
variants.context: Four architectures answer different questions. Request-response returns one decision before the caller's deadline. An event stream consumes durable events and emits predictions continuously. Micro-batching accumulates compatible requests under a bounded wait. Precompute or edge serves a recent prediction near the caller.
variants.prompt: One interactive caller waits on a decision, and feature retrieval, queueing, inference, policy, and serialization must all fit in the same budget. Which architecture fits?
options: Precompute or edge, so the caller reads a stored result.
Request-response, returning one decision before the caller's deadline.
Micro-batching, so utilization improves under the same deadline.
optionFeedback: A stored result only works when the answer is reusable, which an interactive personal decision usually is not.
Correct: one caller, one deadline, and every stage sharing that budget is the request-response contract.
Batching adds a wait that comes out of the very budget the caller is holding.
variants.hint: Count who is waiting and what has to happen before they can be answered.
variants.explanation: In request-response every stage shares one budget, so the deadline is a property of the whole path rather than of the model call.

variants.title: Place the cache
variants.context: Cache placement is a design decision with failure modes. In-process is fastest but duplicates memory and dies with the replica, distributed memory is shared but is still a dependency, an edge cache needs a safe reusable key, and some predictions must not be cached at all.
variants.prompt: Match each cache strategy to the trade it makes.

pairs.label: In-process
pairs.detail: Fastest read, but memory is duplicated per replica and entries die on restart.

pairs.label: Distributed memory
pairs.detail: Shared across servers, but still a dependency with timeout and hot-key failures.

pairs.label: Edge cache
pairs.detail: Closest to the caller, but only for results whose key can encode privacy and version.

pairs.label: No prediction cache
pairs.detail: Runs inference every time, so features and runtime are what get optimized.

variants.hint: Every cache moves the result closer and adds a way for it to be wrong.
variants.explanation: Cache placement changes latency and scope together, so the choice follows from reusability, privacy, and how the result is invalidated.

variants.title: Place the cache
variants.context: Cache placement is a design decision with failure modes. In-process is fastest but duplicates memory and dies with the replica, distributed memory is shared but is still a dependency, an edge cache needs a safe reusable key, and some predictions must not be cached at all.
variants.prompt: Match each workload to the cache strategy it calls for.

pairs.label: Small bounded values that are cheap to recompute
pairs.detail: Keep them in the serving process itself.

pairs.label: Feature vectors many servers in a region need
pairs.detail: Share them from a regional memory tier.

pairs.label: A popular public result with a versioned key
pairs.detail: Serve it from the edge, near the caller.

pairs.label: A personal score over rapidly changing inputs
pairs.detail: Do not cache the prediction at all.

variants.hint: Ask who else can safely see this exact result.
variants.explanation: Predictions that depend on private, high-cardinality, rapidly changing, or non-deterministic inputs are not cacheable, so the work goes into features and runtime instead.

variants.title: Place the cache
variants.context: Cache placement is a design decision with failure modes. In-process is fastest but duplicates memory and dies with the replica, distributed memory is shared but is still a dependency, an edge cache needs a safe reusable key, and some predictions must not be cached at all.
variants.prompt: Match each production symptom to the cause it points at.

pairs.label: Hit rate collapses after every deploy
pairs.detail: The cache lives inside the replica and restarts with it.

pairs.label: One key saturates a single cache node
pairs.detail: A shared tier is carrying a hot-key pattern.

pairs.label: Two users see each other's result
pairs.detail: The edge key does not encode the identity it should.

pairs.label: Latency is fine but predictions are stale
pairs.detail: Invalidation is not keeping up with the model version.

variants.hint: Each symptom names the place the result was stored.
variants.explanation: A cache is a dependency with its own failure modes, so timeouts, hot keys, invalidation, and key design are monitored rather than assumed.
